# Transparent by Law: 20 Years of the Freedom of Information Principle in Figures

> Access requests to the federal administration have more than tripled since 2015. In 2025, however, full access was granted in only 39% of cases, and the number of statutory exemptions is growing.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/transparent-per-gesetz/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Since 1 July 2006, documents of the federal administration have in principle been public, and since 1 November 2023 access has in principle been free of charge. Demand has risen sharply: in 2025 the federal authorities reported 2,145 processed access requests, almost four times as many as in 2015. At the same time, the share of requests with full access fell to 39%, and the Federal Council and Parliament have exempted 13 areas from the Act entirely. Sweden and Estonia show what openness as the norm looks like.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The federal figures come from the activity reports of the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC), most recently the 33rd report 2025/2026 with the statistics on access requests under the Freedom of Information Act (BGÖ/FoIA) for calendar year 2025. The authorities report their cases themselves; the FDPIC points out that the workload is not recorded consistently. There are no comparable overall statistics for Sweden and Estonia; the comparison is therefore limited to the statutory rules. Cantonal laws and Parliament itself do not fall under the FoIA.

---

### Demand is growing

In the first (half) year, 2006, 95 requests were received; in 2015 there were 600, in 2024 a peak of 2,232 and in 2025 2,145 (2,086 new plus 59 carried over from the previous year). According to the FDPIC, the annual number has more than tripled in ten years. Fees are the exception: in 2025 the federal authorities charged a total of 7,601 francs.

---

### Less full access

The share of requests with full access was stable at around 50% from 2020 to 2024 and fell to 39% in 2025. Partial or deferred access rose to 25%, while complete refusals remained at around 10%. Cases where no official document existed (13%) and pending requests (9%) rose sharply. The FDPIC also observes that the FoIA is sometimes used for purposes unrelated to transparency.

---

### Mediation takes too long

Anyone who disagrees with an authority's decision can request mediation from the FDPIC; in 2025 there were 203 requests. The law provides 30 days for this. In 2018 and 2019 the FDPIC met this deadline in about half of cases, since 2022 only in around a quarter (2025: 24%); 36% took more than 100 days. When mediation does take place, it is often successful: 73% of sessions ended in agreement.

---

### Exemptions and comparison

- **Growing exemptions:** since 2006 the Federal Council and Parliament have inserted 13 exemptions in special legislation, and according to the FDPIC at least 11 more are planned, often for supervisory authorities.
- **Sweden:** the principle of public access has applied since the Freedom of the Press Ordinance of 1766 and is now enshrined in Chapter 2 of the Tryckfrihetsförordningen (1949:105) [Freedom of the Press Act], i.e. at constitutional level. Authorities must release records promptly ("skyndsamt"); exemptions are listed exhaustively in the Public Access to Information and Secrecy Act.
- **Estonia:** the Public Information Act requires authorities to maintain publicly accessible electronic document registers; requests must be answered within five working days and are in principle free of charge.

### Interests and terms of office

Members of the Federal Assembly must disclose their professional activities, mandates and advisory functions and, since December 2019, state whether a mandate is paid or unpaid (Art. 11 ParlA). The Parliamentary Services publish the register online. The amount of remuneration does not have to be disclosed. There are no term limits at federal level, but there are in some cantons: in the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt, a four-year break is required after 16 years; in the Landrat of Basel-Landschaft, members who have served four consecutive terms may not stand for the next one (§ 54 KV BL [cantonal constitution]).

---

## What this means for policy

- **Justify exemptions and give them a time limit:** every new exemption from the FoIA with a public justification and an expiry date; the existing 13 are reviewed: [Open Government](https://die-zukunft.ch/en/open-government/).
- **Proactive rather than on request:** document registers on the Estonian model, so that documents do not have to be requested individually in the first place.
- **Meet deadlines:** resource the FDPIC so that the 30-day deadline is the rule again; measure it publicly every year.
- **Put a figure on interests:** disclose income from mandates in bands; examine term limits on the Basel model.

---
